newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Patriarch says NATO should also bring in Orthodox.
newsitem.headline: Patriarch says NATO should also bring in Orthodox.

text.p: NATO's expansion to former East bloc states should not create a new divide between Catholics and Protestants in the west and the Orthodox in east Europe, the Orthodox Church's leading moral authority said.

The warning from Bartholomew, Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, in an interview published on Monday, was tantamount to supporting the longshot bid of mainly Orthodox Romania to join NATO among first-wave entrants.
"Preserving the unity of Europe is the foremost duty of all churches today," Bartholomew told the Bucharest daily Adevarul.

"The opinion now prevailing in some Western circles is the return towards some kind of isolationism of the Western world, seen by some as genuinely Roman Catholic or Protestant," said Bartholomew, spiritual leader of 250 million Orthodox Christians worldwide.
"This aims to create a new division of Europe and to have only countries with a Roman Catholic or Protestant tradition admitted to NATO."
Many of Romania's 22 million people fear that being denied rapid entry to the Atlantic Alliance could leave the country out in the cold seven years after throwing off communist rule.

Romania is the only ex-communist Orthodox country with a chance of securing early membership. But its bid lags behind those of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- where Catholics or Protestants are predominant.
"At this stage Romania does not have great (admission) prospects, particularly if it is used as a tool to continue the division of the Orthodox world," said Bartholomew.

Romania has won support from France, Italy and Canada to be invited to join when the Alliance announces the successful candidates at a Madrid summit in July. But the United States and Britain have been reluctant to back its bid.

Romanian Patriarch Teoctist last month urged fellow Orthodox clerics from the United States and Canada, as well as from Greece, NATO's only Orthodox member, to back Romania's bid. He said it would "help a better understanding of Orthodox values in the world".
The Orthodox world has been riven by rifts involving the Russian Orthodox Church over its continued rule over churches in Estonia and other ex-Soviet states since the fall of communism.

Russian Patriarch Alexiy II has joined in the Kremlin's hostility to an extended NATO. He told U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in February that Russians were "unified in their opposition to NATO expansion".
Pope John Paul, a Pole widely seen as a key figure behind the fall of communism, blessed Poland's membership bid, Polish President Alexander Kwasniewski said at the Vatican last month.

The Pope, spiritual leader of the world's 960 million Roman Catholics, might hold a historic meeting in Austria next month with both Bartholomew and Alexiy, who commands allegiance from some 100 million Orthodox Russians.
The meeting would be the first between a Pope and Orthodox church leaders since Christendom was split into Greek and Latin churches during the Great Schism of 1054.
